deep.reconstruction:
The page is a bare two-column table headed 'Erste Reihe' (first series). It contains no derivation.

Each line gives a star name, then an angle in degrees, minutes and seconds (column A), and sometimes a second angle (column B). All the stars are circumpolar: Draco, Cepheus, and Ursa (almost certainly Ursa Minor, since α Ursae = Polaris and β Ursae = Kochab). Horizontal rules divide the list into three groups.

Column A rises monotonically:
- 36 Dra 6°37'6"; 34 Cep 7°48'; 80 Dra 18°46'4"; 7 (or η) Cep 19°30'34"; θ/6 Cep 20°13'19".
- ι Cep 24°44'1"; h Urs 26°8'25"; α Urs 27°15'26" (written small, interlinear, as an insertion); 25 Cep 28°4'58"; α Cep 28°9'43"; δ Cep 32°29'8".
- ε Urs 32°37'44"; ζ Cep 32°39'53"; l(?) Urs 33°4'21"; β Urs 37°28'18"; ψ Urs 44°27'32".

Column B is written in full only at a few anchor lines: 76°54'58" (36 Dra), 76°53'44" (δ Cep), 76°52'34" (β Urs), 76°49'2" (ψ Urs). The other lines give only a trailing figure. The reading that fits best is seconds carried over from the anchor above: 44, 40, 36, 23, 16, 14, 14 for the first two groups, i.e. 76°54'44" … 76°54'14". For ε Urs, ζ Cep and l Urs (24, 42, 29), the minute is ambiguous, so the sequence is not clearly monotone there. Overall, column B falls slowly by about 6' while column A grows by about 38°.

Interpretation (mine, tentative): column A is a running coordinate along a 'row' of stars, and column B is a nearly constant companion quantity. Possibilities include:
- reduced readings of a fixed instrument;
- an arc-angle or inclination for stars lying near a common great circle;
- the second vernier or zenith-distance reading in an observing series.

Column A is not right ascension, declination, or ecliptic longitude for 1800. For example, α Cep and δ Cep differ by about 18° in RA but by 4°19' here. The page offers no formula, so the purpose cannot be reconstructed with certainty. It is observational or catalogue bookkeeping, probably tied to Gauss's early astronomical work around 1800.
errors: No computations are shown, so no mathematical errors can be identified.

Column B is not visibly monotone in the third group (ε Urs '24', ζ Cep '42', l Urs '29'); the minute is ambiguous. This may be an observing scatter, or the abbreviated entries may imply a minute change that is not written.
The entry for 34 Cephei is incomplete (7°48' only, no seconds, no column B).

results.what: Table of angular values (two columns) for about 16 circumpolar stars in Draco, Cepheus and Ursa Minor, labelled 'Erste Reihe'
results.modern_name: Star observation / reduction table (positional astronomy bookkeeping)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a plain data table of star positions or instrument readings with no derivation or method. Such observational bookkeeping is entirely routine for Gauss's astronomical notebooks around 1800.
